title: Using exec to define a member function that uses super()
author: crj
jonathandung
text: Why would you want to do this?

author: crj
text:
To mechanically generate complex member functions.
Yes, you could eval() the entire class, or generate an entire .py file, but this is a case where most of the code is straightforward and I only want to generate one or two functions.
An ugly workaround is to Base.method(self, ...) instead of super().method(...), but I confess at this point I’m at least as interested in filling a hole in my knowledge concerning how classes are built and whether that functionality is user-accessible.
Having prodded things a little more, I infer that:

The special behaviour is implemented in compiling the AST to bytecode
It seems to be triggered by the presence of a Name('super') within the syntax of a function definition within a class.

Honestly, that feels a tiny bit hacky…

author: effigies
text: I don’t think exec was designed for this type of thing, and I would instead look into metaclasses. But could you show examples of the real sorts of methods you’re trying to auto-generate?

author: Rosuav
text:
CRJ:

An ugly workaround is to Base.method(self, ...) instead of super().method(...), but I confess at this point I’m at least as interested in filling a hole in my knowledge concerning how classes are built and whether that functionality is user-accessible.


Are you able to use the two-arg version instead? super(Derived, self).whatever() ? The zero-arg version is a very nice convenience, but it’s ultimately syntactic sugar for that. (The class name is whatever one you’re currently defining, no need to pick a base class or anything.)

author: DavidCEllis
text:
There are a few ways you can make an exec-ed function work with a no arg super, although it’s a little sneaky.
Essentially you want to get your function from inside a function that defines __class__ inside the string you’re exec-ing with a way to reassign __class__. Providing you don’t need to actually perform your exec call or assignment inside the class body you can do something like this.
s = """
def maker(__class__):
    def f(self):
        super().f()
        print(f"and {type(self).__name__}")
    return f
"""
globs = {}
exec(s, globs)
maker = globs["maker"]

class Base:
    def f(self):
        print(f"From Base")

class Derived(Base):
    pass

Derived.f = maker(Derived)
Derived().f()

From Base
and Derived

It’s also possible to patch __class__ inside the closure cell from a method defined on another class (you can see this kind of work in dataclasses where methods on a dataclass are patched to work on a new slotted copy of the class).
